title: Application Authentication Architecture
description: Learn common application authentication patterns with Cognito, including React apps, API Gateway, and ALB integrations.

data.text: Now that you understand Cognito User Pools and Identity Pools, let us look at how they fit into real application architectures. There are two common patterns: API Gateway + Lambda, and ALB + ECS.
Pattern 1: React → Cognito → API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB

In this serverless pattern, the React app authenticates users via Cognito. The app sends the JWT token with every API request to API Gateway. API Gateway validates the token and forwards the request to Lambda, which reads from or writes to DynamoDB.

data.caption: Serverless auth pattern with React, Cognito, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB

    B -->|2. JWT tokens| A

    C -->|4. Validate token| C
    C -->|5. Forward request| D[Lambda Function]
    D -->|6. Read/Write| E[DynamoDB]
    D -->|7. Response| A

data.text: In this container-based pattern, the React app authenticates users via Cognito. The Application Load Balancer (ALB) is configured with Cognito authentication. When users access the app, ALB redirects them to Cognito for sign-in and then forwards authenticated requests to ECS containers.

data.title: Best Practices
items: Always validate JWT tokens on the server side
Use short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens
Store tokens securely — use HttpOnly cookies for web apps
Use Identity Pools only when users need direct AWS access

data.title: Architecture Tip
data.text: For most web applications, Pattern 1 (API Gateway + Lambda) is simpler and more cost-effective. Use Pattern 2 (ALB + ECS) when you need containerized workloads or want to migrate existing applications.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Serverless pattern uses API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB
Container pattern uses ALB + ECS with Cognito auth
Always validate JWT tokens on the backend
Choose the pattern that matches your workload
